original_question: Are both Dubin–Johnson syndrome and Rotor syndrome associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

final_qi.question: Is Dubin–Johnson syndrome associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
final_qi.long_answer: Dubin–Johnson syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ABCC2 (MRP2) canalicular transporter. The defect impairs the hepatic excretion of conjugated (direct) bilirubin into the bile. As a result, patients develop a chronic, predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, while unconjugated bilirubin and other liver function tests are usually normal. This association is well documented in hepatology and genetic-metabolic disease literature.

final_qi.question: Is Rotor syndrome associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
final_qi.long_answer: Rotor syndrome is a rare, benign, autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the hepatic transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (genes SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3). The primary biochemical hallmark is a chronic, predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia, similar to but typically milder than that seen in Dubin–Johnson syndrome. Because the defect is in hepatic uptake and storage rather than bilirubin conjugation, bilirubin that has already been conjugated in hepatocytes leaks back into the blood, leading to elevated serum levels of direct (conjugated) bilirubin. This relationship—Rotor syndrome being associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia—is well established in hepatology textbooks and clinical literature.
